summary: MCMit is a hardware-software co-design that mitigates mid-circuit measurement (MCM) errors and classical feedback latency in superconducting quantum processors through a constant-latency multi-qubit branch instruction, two neural network discriminators achieving 62% higher accuracy for 250–500 ns readout, and circuit-level optimization. Implemented on Qubic and evaluated on experimental readout traces, MCMit reduces feedback latency by 70%, improves QEC logical error rates by 1.2–9.4× for surface codes, and delivers 18–30% fidelity gains for distributed quantum computing workloads.
motivation: MCMs suffer from 2–12× higher error rates than two-qubit gates and 23–38× longer durations on IBM Heron/Nighthawk processors, while classical feedback adds 3–10× latency. These bottlenecks severely hinder scalability in DQC architectures and fault tolerance in QEC, yet existing hardware controllers, discriminators, and software techniques operate in isolation without cross-layer co-design.
method: MCMit introduces: (1) an FPGA-based $branch_reduce_fproc$ instruction supporting multi-qubit XOR/majority operations with constant latency independent of qubit count; (2) a transformer and lightweight residual CNN discriminator operating directly on raw I/Q traces via spectral preprocessing and learnable downsampling, with INT8 quantization for FPGA deployment; (3) compile-time static MCM elimination via quantum constant propagation, measurement hardening using repetition codes and parity checks, and stochastic branching that probabilistically inverts branch conditions using confusion matrices.
result: On five-qubit superconducting QPU readout traces: $branch_reduce_fproc$ reduces feedback latency by up to 70% and circuit depth by 7× over Qubic; MCMit-CNN achieves 62.4% higher discrimination accuracy than HERQULES at 500 ns readout (78.8% excluding crosstalk-affected qubits) with 92% lower LUT utilization; surface code logical error rates drop 1.2–9.4× at 500 ns readout; GHZ and CNOT benchmarks show 37.8–57.3% higher fidelity than Qubic; software mitigation achieves 18–30% fidelity improvement over Qiskit mthree and unmitigated circuits.
